newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Jewish camp files said dumped in rubbish.
newsitem.headline: French Jewish camp files said dumped in rubbish.

text.p: French Jews voiced outrage and authorities opened an inquiry on Friday into a report that files from a French wartime internment camp for Jews bound for Nazi death camps had been found on a rubbish tip.
A local newspaper in the southern town of Perpignan said a person who requested anonymity brought the files to its offices, saying he found them on a rubbish dump in a nearby village.

The daily L'Independant de Perpignan said the files included the names of about 1,000 Jews taken between April and December 1942 to and from the infamous Rivesaltes camp, in the foothills of the Pyrenees.

Some 2,000 Jews were deported from Rivesaltes to Drancy camp in the Paris suburbs which was run by the occupying German forces. It was from Drancy that internees were sent to Nazi death camps where most were killed on arrival in gas chambers.
Bernard Bonnet, the prefect (government representative) in Perpignan, called in a representative of the local Jewish community to express indignation.

France's top Jewish religious body, the consistory, said the documents could help clarify the responsibility of the wartime collaborationist Vichy government in the Holocaust ahead of the trial of former minister Maurice Papon.
Papon, 86, is to go on trial in October on charges of crimes against humanity for ordering the deportation of 1,560 Jews from southwest France to death camps.
The umbrella group of Jewish community organisations, CRIF, voiced outrage and asked authorities to draw up an inventory of all archives about the Rivesaltes camp.

The director of public archives in Perpignan, Marie-Edith de Lavergnee, told a news conference all archives regarding World War Two internees in the region were in her possession and none had been stolen.
"Collective memory has been seriously outraged. I hope justice will rapidly shed light on this case," she said.
A state prosecutor opened a preliminary inquiry.
Nazi hunter Serge Klarsfeld said the files appeared to be copies of documents he had consulted previously at the local archives.

He believed the copies may have been hidden at the end of World War Two by a local civil servant or an employee of the Rivesaltes camp. Heirs may have found them recently and decided to get rid of them.

The newspaper report said the files included lists of Jews sent from Rivesaltes to Drancy, of others provisionally excluded from convoys, police reports on detentions, and correspondance between Vichy and regional authorities.
The newspaper said it received the files a few weeks ago but held its report until Thursday May 8 to coincide with the 52nd anniversary of Germany's World War Two surrender.
